title: staged-reveal-fewshot-dialectic-notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working scratchpad exploring a staged-reveal few-shot strategy where examples are introduced incrementally (a dialectic) rather than all up-front. Goal: improve helpfulness and reduce early hallucination when working under tight token budgets and variable user context lengths.

Background and motivation:
- Problem: long few-shot contexts blow token budgets and often surface noisy exemplars early, biasing the model toward wrong patterns. Some failure modes we see: premature pattern lock, answer sprawl, and inconsistent adherence to constraints when prompts include many long examples.
- Hypothesis: reveal small, highly targeted exemplars first to set the scaffolding, then inject corrective or edge-case exemplars only when the model shows ambiguity (either by asking a clarifying question or producing low-confidence signals). This mimics a teacher-student dialectic.

High-level staged flow (prototype):
1) Minimal seed: system + 1 compact exemplar (3–4 lines). Keep token cost <= 80 tokens.
2) Ask the model to attempt the task with an instruction that allows a short answer. Collect the output and a confidence proxy (see below).
3) If confidence < threshold or answer contains hallmarks (hallucination keywords, inconsistent formatting), append a second exemplar demonstrating error recovery + a short, direct corrective instruction.
4) Re-run with appended exemplar (only one extra).
5) If still bad, append a third exemplar (edge-case) and enable a soft fallback route (e.g., call tool to retrieve facts or switch to smaller model for verification).

Confidence proxy ideas (cheap signals):
- Generation length vs expected length (abnormally long may be sprawl).
- Presence of hedging words like "I think" "maybe" when instruction asked for definitive answer.
- Fallback token for deterministic checks: ask final token whether it used outside knowledge tokens (simple heuristic).
- Model logprob if available (use per-token average).

Example templates (compact):
-- System: You are an assistant that answers in a single paragraph and cites when outside knowledge is needed.
-- Exemplar 1 (seed):
Q: "Summarize the user policy for canceling a paid subscription in one sentence."
A: "Users can cancel anytime from their account settings; billing stops at the end of the current paid period (no prorate)."
(3 lines)

-- Instruction for attempt: "Respond in one sentence. If you need to look up policy details, say 'needs lookup'."

If output contains "needs lookup" or diverges format, append exemplar 2:
Exemplar 2 (recovery):
Q: "How do refunds work after cancellation?"
A: "Refunds are only issued for billing errors; standard cancellations do not trigger refunds."

Edge-case exemplar 3 (if still failing):
Q: "What happens to invoices if a subscription is canceled mid-month?"
A: "Invoices already generated remain; future invoices stop. Please check billing history for specifics."

Observed failure modes to track in experiments:
- Split-attention: model repeats instruction but ignores the small exemplar once an edge-case exemplar is appended.
- Overfitting: model parrots exemplar wording even when inappropriate.
- Instability on short prompts: staged reveal helps some tasks but hurts others (classification vs generation).

Evaluation plan (iteration-friendly):
- Metric set (automated):
  * Exact-match for strict tasks (labels, short answers).
  * BLEU / ROUGE for summaries (low weight).
  * Hallucination score: fraction of outputs with unsupported facts (via small fact-check tool).
  * Token cost per successful example (median).
  * Attempt count (how often staged flow needs 2nd/3rd exemplar).
- Human eval: 3-point rubric (correct/acceptable/wrong) sampled 200 items per condition.
- A/B: compare full few-shot (3 exemplars upfront) vs staged reveal with same exemplar set.

Edge-case checklist for creating exemplars:
- Make seed exemplar minimal and prototypical (avoid extraneous context).
- Recovery exemplar demonstrates explicit error-correction, not just another positive case.
- Edge-case exemplar should be short and target common failure surfaces.
- Do not leak sensitive details in exemplars.

Runtime considerations / implementation notes:
- Orchestration: lightweight client-side logic. Try local orchestration first before embedding into Redwood routes.
- Cache: cache the seed exemplar + result; only append if necessary. Cache key: (instruction hash, user_context_truncation_hash).
- Latency: each additional exemplar is a new model call; should cap at 2 extra calls for interactive UX. Consider a batch mode for high-throughput workloads where staged reveal is simulated by single-call concatenation with token markers indicating reveal order.
- Cost: compute expected tokens saved vs extra calls. Hypothesis: for low-error workloads staged reveal reduces average tokens by avoiding long upfront example blocks.

Sample experiment matrix (short):
- Task types: classification (multi-choice), short-answer (1–2 sentences), summarization (1–3 sentences), instruction-following.
- Models: small (opt-1), mid (redwood-medium), large (redwood-large) — aim to see when staged reveal helps.
- Context length buckets: 0–128, 129–512, 513–2048 tokens.
- Conditions: (A) full 3-exemplar upfront, (B) staged reveal up to 2 reveals, (C) staged reveal + verification tool.

Notes from quick pilot (raw findings):
- For classification, staged reveal reduced sprawl and increased exact-match by ~4% on a 1k sample using mid model (seed exemplar good).
- For summarization, staged reveal hurt some cases: when the model needed style calibration, upfront examples were better. Maybe mixing: front-load one style exemplar and stage content-focused exemplars.
- Token savings observed when typical dialogues are short (<150 tokens): saving ~60–120 tokens per request on average vs full upfront 3-exemplar set.

Open questions and next steps:
- How to reliably measure "model asks a clarifying question" without human labeling? Maybe a short probe: if first-generation contains a question mark and specific keywords, treat as clarifier.
- Should exemplars be paraphrased on second reveal to avoid parroting? Test paraphrase vs exact copy.
- Combine with lightweight reranker: after each attempt, run a rules-based filter for hallucination triggers.
- Design rollout for Redwood: start as a client SDK sample and then bake into Redwood Optimize suggestions if metrics look promising.

Small action items (next 2 weeks):
- [ ] Implement pilot harness that supports staged reveals and confidence proxies (assign: Lena).
- [ ] Create 3 representative datasets (classification, short-answer, summarization) from existing prompt bank (assign: me).
- [ ] Run baseline vs staged reveal on mid model for 1k items each (assign: Miles).
- [ ] Collate failure examples and draft exemplar template guidelines (assign: me + Lena).

Notes-to-self: keep exemplars terse, track token spend per API call explicitly, and avoid building show-stopper orchestration into server until we have consistent gains. Also: capture example ids so we can A/B the exact same exemplars when comparing upfront vs staged.
